newsitem.title: USA: Pension funds not following Philadelphia on Texaco.
newsitem.headline: Pension funds not following Philadelphia on Texaco.

text.p: Public pension funds that own stock in Texaco Inc. have no plans to follow the lead of the city of Philadelphia's pension board and divest their shares in the oil giant, state and city officials said Friday.

The Philadelphia pension board voted Thursday to divest $5.5 million worth of Texaco stock, citing evidence of racial bias at the oil company. The divestiture came after revelations that tape recordings of discussions among Texaco executives were laced with racial slurs.
The move comes a week after the Philadelphia City Council voted in a non-binding resolution to boycott Texaco and divest itself of all holdings in the oil company.
The Texaco tapes came to light in connection with a racial discrimination lawsuit filed against Texaco by six black employees.

State and city pension funds indicated that, while they were outraged by the revelations of apparent racism, they preferred to work with Texaco management to correct any problems rather than sell their stakes.
"We are extremely concerned about the recent events at Texaco," said a spokesman for New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi, noting that Hevesi met Texaco Chairman Peter Bijur earlier in the week.
A spokeswoman for New Jersey's treasurer, Brian Clymer, said there were no plans to sell its 990,000 shares. The funds have a market value of about $54 billion.

Connecticut's state treasurer, Christopher Burnham, who is sole fiduciary for the $14.2 billion fund, views its $43.7 million stake in Texaco stock as a passive investment as part of its overall investment in all of the issues in the S&P 500 index, according to a spokesman.
Rhode Island Treasurer Nancy Mayer also has no plans to divest the 21,400 shares out of its $4.4 billion Employees Retirement System of Rhode Island, a spokesman said.

Tim Smith, executive director of the New York-based Interfaith Centre on Corporate Responsibility, which represents religious institutions with about $50 billion in assets, said it was urging that holders keep their Texaco stock.

Smith said the group would seek a variety of changes at Texaco, including diversifying the makeup of the board and reviewing the "glass ceiling" that it says may prevent promotions for women and minorities.

At least one "socially responsible" mutual fund, which owns Texaco shares, is also keeping its stake. Frank Rauscher, chief executive officer of the $53 million Aquinas Equity Income Fund, which calls itself a fund that follows the values of the Roman Catholic church, said it would hold its 10,000 shares.

"Our approach to social investing is that, as holders, we have more voice than as non-shareholders," Rauscher said. "We will use our shareholder position to assure that Texaco works to keep its commitment with regards to employment practices."

Texaco last week reached a $176 million settlement of a 1994 lawsuit brought by a group of black employees accusing the company of systematically discriminating against blacks and denying them promotions. It was the biggest settlement of a discrimination case in the United States.
A former Texaco executive was charged by federal authorities Tuesday with obstructing justice by destroying documents sought in the racial discrimination case.
White Plains, N.Y.-based Texaco, meanwhile, faces a consumer boycott due to the allegations of discrimination.
Texaco stock rose $1.50 to $100.375 Friday on the New York Stock Exchange.
